"Everyone" shows how complete the judgment would be. It would not stop with a defeated army or a few captured towns, but would reach throughout the land. "Cut off" is a strong word for destruction, and Obadiah uses it again for Edom's future (1:10) and for what Edom did to Judah's survivors (1:14). Edom would suffer the same fate it had brought on others.
9.notes:
The Hebrew text that the NKJV follows ends verse 9 with the words "by slaughter." The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation (as printed in Brenton's 1851 edition), places the word for slaughter at the start of verse 10 instead, so that verse 10 begins roughly, "because of the slaughter and the ungodliness against your brother Jacob." The NRSV follows that arrangement, opening verse 10 with "For the slaughter and violence done to your brother Jacob." The NET Bible also joins slaughter to verse 10.

The Hebrew consonants are the same either way. The question is only where the sentence breaks. The NKJV's arrangement is well supported and reads naturally. It says that Edom would be "cut off by slaughter." The other reading would make verse 10 name slaughter alongside violence as Edom's crime.

reflections.title: Courage Is Not a Personality Trait
reflections.html: “Then your mighty men will be dismayed, O Teman.” “Dismayed” means shattered, terrified, the very word God uses when He tells Joshua, “Do not tremble or be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you” (Joshua 1:9). Teman was known for fierce warriors, yet the seasoned, hardened soldiers would tremble like frightened children, like the panic from God that fell on the Philistines (1 Samuel 14:15). What God forbids His people because of His presence, He sends on those who trust in themselves. Physical strength and military training dissolve into dismay; courage evaporates when the Lord withdraws His hand. Teman’s warriors lost heart before they lost the battle. Courage is an unearned gift and the fruit of God’s presence, not of a strong constitution.
reflections.q: “Then your mighty men will be dismayed, O Teman.”

reflections.title: Room Left for a Remnant
reflections.html: Teman, named for Esau’s grandson (Genesis 36:11), stands for the whole nation, and “everyone” in Hebrew idiom often means the nation as a whole. That leaves room for the remnant of Edom that Amos foresaw coming under the name of the LORD (Amos 9:12). Even a sweeping sentence on a nation does not close the door on its people.
reflections.q: Teman, named for Esau’s grandson (Genesis 36:11), stands for the whole nation, and “everyone” in Hebrew idiom often means the nation as a whole.

10.brief: Now the reason for the judgment is named: “violence against your brother Jacob.” Because Edom turned on the nation descended from its own brother, shame will cover it and it will be cut off forever.
10.explain:
"For violence against your brother Jacob,"

"For" gives the reason behind the judgment announced in the previous verses. The Hebrew word for "violence" describes cruel, ruthless wrongdoing that tramples on others. It is the word used when "the earth was filled with violence" before the flood (Genesis 6:11). Joel names the same sin when he says Edom would become "a desolate wilderness, because of violence against the people of Judah" (Joel 3:19). The verses that follow spell out what this violence looked like: Edom gloated over Judah's ruin, joined in the looting, and handed over people trying to escape (11–14).

What made Edom's violence especially wicked is that it was done to a brother. Edom descended from Esau, and Israel descended from Esau's twin brother, Jacob. The two boys struggled even in their mother's womb, and the LORD told Rebekah, "Two nations are in your womb" (Genesis 25:23). Esau became the father of the Edomites (Genesis 36:1), and Jacob, whom God renamed Israel (Genesis 32:28), became the father of the twelve tribes. "Jacob" here means the people of Israel, and especially Judah, whose capital, Jerusalem, suffered the attack Obadiah describes.

The two nations never forgot they were related. When Israel traveled toward the Promised Land, Moses sent word to the king of Edom, "Thus says your brother Israel" (Numbers 20:14). God told His people, "You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother" (Deuteronomy 23:7). Israel was commanded to treat Edom as family, but Edom treated Israel as an enemy. Amos condemned Edom because "he pursued his brother with the sword, and cast off all pity" (Amos 1:11). The bond between them should have moved Edom to help. Instead, it made Edom's cruelty a betrayal.

"Shame shall cover you,"

Shame would wrap around Edom like a garment until nothing else could be seen. Edom had been a proud nation, confident in its mountain strongholds and admired for its wisdom. It had looked on Judah's humiliation with contempt, but the disgrace Edom enjoyed watching would now cover Edom itself. A nation that prized its honor would be remembered for how it treated its brother.

"And you shall be cut off forever."

To "cut off" means to be destroyed and removed, like a branch cut from a tree. The word "forever" shows that Edom's fall would be permanent. It would not recover and rise again as a nation. This stands in sharp contrast to the end of the prophecy, where God promises that Jacob will be delivered and restored (17–21). Both peoples would suffer, but only Israel had a future promised by God. Edom did in time disappear as a distinct nation. The judgment falls on Edom as a people and a kingdom; it does not mean that every individual descended from Esau died. Nor does Obadiah tie its fulfillment to a single moment in history, for he goes on to place Edom's judgment within the day of the LORD upon all the nations (1:15).

reflections.title: God Shows His Reasons
reflections.html: “Because of violence to your brother Jacob.” The word “because” turns the book into a courtroom: God does not strike arbitrarily; He lays out the evidence. The charge is chamas, violent wrong, the word that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11, 13) and the word Habakkuk cried out against (Habakkuk 1:2). Judgment flows from God’s goodness, not against it. A God who never named violence and never answered it would not be good.
reflections.q: “Because of violence to your brother Jacob.”

reflections.title: The Law of Brotherhood
reflections.html: The indictment pivots here. Edom’s great sin was not merely pride; it was the violation of blood ties. Esau and Jacob were twins, and God remembers family bonds. God measures our spiritual integrity by how we treat our brothers and sisters, especially in their moments of weakness.
reflections.q: The indictment pivots here.

reflections.title: Your Brother Jacob
reflections.html: The victim is not called “Judah” but “your brother Jacob.” Israel had been commanded, “You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7), and Esau had once run to Jacob, embraced him, and wept on his neck (Genesis 33:4). Edom’s descendants reopened the wound their forefather had closed; Amos says Edom “cast off all pity” and “kept his wrath forever” (Amos 1:11). Sins against family carry extra weight because they betray a bond God Himself gave. The nearer the relationship, the heavier the violence weighs on God’s scale.
reflections.q: The victim is not called “Judah” but “your brother Jacob.”

reflections.title: Covered With the Opposite of What You Wore
reflections.html: “Shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever.” In verse 3 Edom was wrapped in pride; now it is wrapped in shame, the garment of the humbled (Micah 7:10). Ezekiel calls Edom’s hatred an “ancient” and “perpetual” enmity (Ezekiel 35:5), and the sentence matches it: an enmity kept forever ends in being cut off forever. God’s sentences are not always completed at once; Edom’s unwound over centuries until the Idumeans vanished from history after A.D. 70. A grudge nursed for a lifetime does not stay small. It becomes who we are, and then it becomes our verdict. Is there an old family or church wound we have kept alive for years, that we need to let God close instead of reopening it?
reflections.q: Is there an old family or church wound we have kept alive for years, that we need to let God close instead of reopening it?

reflections.title: When Family Bitterness Festers
reflections.html: The blood feud reached back over a thousand years to the struggle in Rebekah’s womb (Genesis 25:22–23). Unattended family bitterness and generational jealousy fester into corporate, destructive hatred that finally brings down the judgment of God. Is there a family grudge, a sibling feud, or an old root of bitterness that we are keeping alive? What step of reconciliation or radical forgiveness must we take now, before it poisons the next generation?
reflections.q: What step of reconciliation or radical forgiveness must we take now, before it poisons the next generation?

11.brief: On the day foreigners entered Jerusalem’s gates, carried away its forces, and cast lots for the city, most likely Babylon’s conquest in 586 BC, Edom “stood on the other side” instead of helping its brother. God counts that stance as joining the enemy: “Even you were as one of them.”
11.explain:
"In the day that you stood on the other side—"

The LORD is still speaking to Edom, the nation descended from Esau, and here He points to a specific day. In Hebrew this is literally "in the day of your standing opposite," a picture of someone keeping his distance and watching. The same kind of language appears when David grieves that "my loved ones and my friends stand aloof from my plague, and my relatives stand afar off" (Psalm 38:11). Edom watched from a distance while its brother was being destroyed. That is serious enough on its own, because Israel had been told, "You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother" (Deuteronomy 23:7). Edom owed Judah the same loyalty and gave none.

"In the day that strangers carried captive his forces,"

"His" refers to Jacob, that is, the people of Israel, the brother Edom wronged (v. 10). Obadiah does not name the invaders. Most likely they were the Babylonians, who captured Jerusalem in 586 BC. King Nebuchadnezzar's army broke through the city wall, burned the temple and the great houses, and carried the people into exile in Babylon (2 Kings 25:1–11). The Hebrew word translated "forces" can mean an army or strength, but it can also mean wealth. The same word is translated "substance" in verse 13. If the invaders were the Babylonians, both happened that day. Judah's people were led away as captives, and its treasures, including the bronze and gold from the temple, were hauled off to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13–17).

"When foreigners entered his gates"

A city's gates were its main defense. When enemies walked through them, the city had fallen. Jerusalem's gates had once stood for the safety of God's people, and now foreign soldiers walked through them freely.

"And cast lots for Jerusalem—"

Conquering armies often cast lots to divide what they had captured, including land, goods, and even people. Joel describes the same cruelty against God's people: "They have cast lots for My people, have given a boy as payment for a harlot, and sold a girl for wine, that they may drink" (Joel 3:3). Jerusalem, the city where God had placed His name, was being divided up like spoils of war.

"Even you were as one of them."

This is the heart of the charge. Strangers carried away Judah's forces, foreigners entered its gates, and lots were cast for Jerusalem, and God says Edom was "as one of them." A brother who stands by while his brother is attacked has already chosen a side. Edom's guilt went beyond watching, too. In the verses that follow, the LORD lists what Edom did: it gloated over Judah's ruin, entered the gate of the fallen city and laid hands on its goods, and stood at the crossroads to cut off those who escaped and hand over those who remained (vv. 12–14). Other passages also remember Edom's hostility when Jerusalem fell. Psalm 137:7 recalls the Edomites shouting, "Raze it, raze it, to its very foundation!" Ezekiel condemns Edom for shedding Israel's blood "at the time of their calamity" (Ezekiel 35:5). Edom should have been the first to help its brother. Instead, it stood with the foreigners.
11.notes:
Obadiah never names the foreigners who entered Jerusalem's gates, so his date has to be worked out from the evidence. The strongest case points to the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Several other passages accuse Edom of hostility when Jerusalem fell (Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21–22; Ezekiel 35:5). The language of captivity, of lots cast for Jerusalem, and of exiles in distant places (v. 20) also fits that disaster well.

An earlier setting has also been proposed: the reign of King Jehoram, about 845 BC, when Edom revolted (2 Kings 8:20–22). In those days the Philistines and Arabians invaded Judah and carried off the king's possessions and his family (2 Chronicles 21:16–17). Supporters point to Obadiah's place between Amos and Jonah in the Bible's order and to the possibility that Jeremiah drew on Obadiah.

However, the account of Jehoram's reign does not mention Edom taking part in that invasion, and although it says the king's house was plundered (2 Chronicles 21:17), it does not describe Jerusalem falling or its people being exiled. For these reasons the Babylonian setting remains the more likely one, though it is not certain.

reflections.title: Standing Aloof Is Standing Somewhere
reflections.html: “On the day that you stood aloof … you too were as one of them.” Literally Edom “stood opposite,” on the other side. Strangers carried off Jerusalem’s wealth, foreigners entered its gates, and Edom watched from across the road. Idle spectators of a neighbor’s troubles, when able to help, have a great deal to answer for. We hear the priest and the Levite who “passed by on the other side” (Luke 10:31–32). God does not accept a chosen distance from a brother’s suffering as neutrality. When the bond is close and the need is clear, the other side of the road is a side.
reflections.q: “On the day that you stood aloof … you too were as one of them.”

reflections.title: The Guilt of the Spectator
reflections.html: Edom did not start the attack on Jerusalem; Babylon did. Edom did not at first swing the sword; it simply stood aloof. Yet the divine verdict is, “you were like one of them.” In God’s kingdom there is no neutral ground regarding the suffering of a brother. Passive complicity in the face of injustice is counted as active participation. To stand by with folded arms while God’s people are crushed is to be charged as a co-conspirator; to do nothing when a brother is crushed is to join the crushers. Withholding love when it is in our power to act is counted as alignment with the enemy. Silence in the face of injustice is complicity, and cold indifference carries the same moral guilt as open hostility. Is there someone in our family, church, or workplace being slandered or mistreated while we watch from across the road and call it neutrality?
reflections.q: Is there someone in our family, church, or workplace being slandered or mistreated while we watch from across the road and call it neutrality?

reflections.title: They Rolled Dice for Jerusalem
reflections.html: “Foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem.” Casting lots was how conquerors divided captives and spoil (Joel 3:3; Nahum 3:10); the city of God was gambled over like loot. The verse climbs: plunder in the countryside, then the gates breached, then lots thrown inside the city. Centuries later soldiers cast lots for the clothing of Jerusalem’s King at the foot of His cross (Psalm 22:18; John 19:24). What the world treats as spoil, God counts as His own, and He keeps the record of who stood by while the dice were thrown.
reflections.q: “Foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem.”

reflections.title: “And You, Brutus?”
reflections.html: The emphatic “you too” has the sting of “And you, Brutus?” The betrayal of a stranger wounds; the betrayal of a brother wounds deeper. One old devotional writer turned the phrase on believers: when we sin, who are the chosen favorites of heaven, we sin with an emphasis.
reflections.q: The emphatic “you too” has the sting of “And you, Brutus?”

12.brief: The repeated rebukes begin with what Edom saw, felt, and said: it should not have gazed on its brother’s day of disaster, rejoiced over the children of Judah, or spoken proudly in their distress. Gloating over a brother’s ruin is already sin in God’s sight, before any hand is raised.
12.explain:
"But you should not have gazed on the day of your brother In the day of his captivity;"

In Hebrew these lines are worded as direct commands. In English they would run something like "Do not gaze... do not rejoice... do not speak." It is as though the LORD stands beside Edom on the day of Jerusalem's fall and tells it to stop. "Gazed" here means more than seeing what happened. It describes looking on with satisfaction, watching another's suffering and enjoying the sight. Edom, the nation descended from Esau, did this on the day of its brother's disaster. The one it watched was its "brother," and that word makes Edom's satisfaction even uglier. A brother should have grieved.

"The day of your brother" means the day of his trouble, the day disaster fell on him. The word translated "captivity" points to that disaster and to the calamity of being overrun. It is related to the word for "foreigners" in the previous verse. The day foreign armies entered Jerusalem's gates was the day Judah's life was overturned and its people were carried away.

"Nor should you have rejoiced over the children of Judah In the day of their destruction;"

Now the satisfaction in Edom's eyes becomes joy in its heart. The LORD names the victims plainly as "the children of Judah," the people of Jerusalem and the southern kingdom. Their day was a day of destruction, when their city was ruined and many perished. Edom celebrated it.

Scripture treats this kind of joy as a serious sin, even against an enemy: "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and do not let your heart be glad when he stumbles; lest the LORD see it, and it displease Him" (Proverbs 24:17–18). It also warns, "He who is glad at calamity will not go unpunished" (Proverbs 17:5). Edom's gladness was not a private feeling God overlooked. Ezekiel recorded the LORD's response: "As you rejoiced because the inheritance of the house of Israel was desolate, so I will do to you" (Ezekiel 35:15).

"Nor should you have spoken proudly In the day of distress."

From the eyes and the heart, Edom's sin came out through its mouth. "Spoken proudly" is literally "made your mouth large." It describes big, boastful talk and mocking words spoken over someone who has fallen. This is the same pride that had already deceived Edom's heart (verse 3), now aimed at a brother who was helpless. Psalm 137 remembers what the Edomites said that day: "Remember, O LORD, against the sons of Edom the day of Jerusalem, who said, 'Raze it, raze it, to its very foundation!'" (Psalm 137:7). Ezekiel adds that God heard every word: "Thus with your mouth you have boasted against Me and multiplied your words against Me; I have heard them" (Ezekiel 35:13). Mocking God's people in their distress was boasting against God Himself.

All through these lines, the word "day" keeps returning: the day of his captivity, the day of their destruction, the day of distress. Edom treated Judah's worst day as an occasion to enjoy, but God was keeping account of that day, and a day of reckoning was coming for Edom as well (verse 15).

reflections.title: Gloating Starts in the Eyes
reflections.html: “Do not gloat over your brother’s day.” The verb is simply “look,” but with its preposition it means to look on with satisfaction, to feast the eyes. Edom’s slide began not with its hands but with its eyes. Savoring the discipline or ruin of a brother is an immediate insult to God’s mercy. “Do not rejoice when your enemy falls … lest the LORD see it, and it displease Him” (Proverbs 24:17–18): while we are watching a brother fall, God is watching our face. Jesus looked at Jerusalem in its coming day of calamity and wept (Luke 19:41). What happens in our eyes when someone falls shows whose heart we have.
reflections.q: “Do not gloat over your brother’s day.”

reflections.title: The Danger of Schadenfreude
reflections.html: There is a deep, fleshly sickness that secretly delights in the failure or suffering of rivals. God forbids us to rejoice when others fall, even when we feel they deserve it; Proverbs warns that if we do, the Lord may turn His anger away from them (Proverbs 24:18). Whose fall have we secretly enjoyed, a rival, a competitor, someone who hurt us, and what did that pleasure reveal about our hearts? How can we learn Christlike grief over their stumbling instead of gloating?
reflections.q: How can we learn Christlike grief over their stumbling instead of gloating?

reflections.title: The Day He Became a Stranger
reflections.html: “The day of his misfortune” uses a word found only here, built on the root “to be strange, foreign”; the KJV renders it “the day that he became a stranger.” On that day Judah was made a foreigner in its own city, handled by strangers as if it belonged to no one. The one neighbor who was not a stranger, the brother, chose that day to treat him like one. There are days when a person needs someone who still knows his name. God calls His people to be that someone, because He Himself has promised never to treat His own as strangers (Isaiah 49:15–16).
reflections.q: “The day of his misfortune” uses a word found only here, built on the root “to be strange, foreign”; the KJV renders it “the day that he became a stranger.”

reflections.title: A Mouth Made Large
reflections.html: “Do not boast in the day of their distress” is literally “do not make your mouth great.” The pride of the heart in verse 3 has reached the mouth in verse 12, as it always does: “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). God tells Edom elsewhere, “With your mouth you have boasted against Me and multiplied your words against Me; I have heard them” (Ezekiel 35:13). The tongue that enlarges itself over another’s ruin reveals a heart that has forgotten its own need of mercy. And God is listening.
reflections.q: “Do not boast in the day of their distress” is literally “do not make your mouth great.”

reflections.title: Eight Lines Edom Crossed
reflections.html: Verse 11 describes a finished event; verses 12–14 switch to eight “do not” commands. Some read them as warnings against a repeat, others as the prophet reliving the day: “You should not have …” Either way, each “do not” names a line Edom crossed, and God remembers every one.
reflections.q: Verse 11 describes a finished event; verses 12–14 switch to eight “do not” commands.

13.brief: The charge moves from watching to acting, as Edom entered the gate of the people the LORD calls “My people,” stared at their affliction, and laid hands on their goods. Three times the verse says “in the day of their calamity,” pressing home that Edom took advantage of Judah at its weakest hour.
13.explain:
"You should not have entered the gate of My people"

In Hebrew this line, like the others in verses 12–14, is worded as a direct command, which in English would be "Do not enter." It is as if the LORD were standing at Jerusalem's gate on that terrible day, forbidding Edom to come through. A city's gate was its main entrance and the center of its public life, where people met, traded, and settled disputes.

Two verses earlier, the LORD described the day when "foreigners entered his gates" and then charged Edom, "Even you were as one of them" (1:11). This verse shows part of what that meant. Edom did not stay outside, watching from a distance. It came in through the gate of the fallen city.

The LORD calls the city "the gate of My people." Edom was not simply taking advantage of a weakened neighbor. The people it moved against belonged to God, and He took their mistreatment personally.

"In the day of their calamity."

The word "calamity" means disaster or ruin, the kind that crushes a people. It appears three times in this one verse, and each time the LORD presses the same point: Edom chose the very day Judah was falling. It did not wait for a fair fight or a time of strength. It came when its brother was helpless. Many interpreters also hear a play on words, since the Hebrew for "their calamity" sounds much like the name "Edom." Edom's character is tied to the disaster it exploited. Ezekiel likewise condemned Edom for striking Israel at the time of its calamity (Ezekiel 35:5), and Proverbs warns, "He who is glad at calamity will not go unpunished" (Proverbs 17:5).

"Indeed, you should not have gazed on their affliction"

Verse 12 already charged Edom with gazing on its brother's day of disaster. Now the gazing happens inside the city. The Hebrew carries the sense of "you too," placing Edom alongside the invaders as one more onlooker staring at Judah's suffering. This was not the look of someone heartbroken by what he saw. It was the look of someone enjoying the sight of a hated rival brought low.

"Nor laid hands on their substance"

Edom finally moved from watching to taking. "Substance" refers to wealth and possessions. In verse 11 the same Hebrew word describes what the strangers "carried captive" (there translated "forces"). The invaders hauled away Judah's wealth, and Edom reached for the same goods. It took hold of its brother's goods on the very day of his calamity.

reflections.title: “My People,” Even in the Day of Discipline
reflections.html: “Do not enter the gate of My people in the day of their calamity.” Jerusalem fell because God was disciplining real sin, and Obadiah never pretends otherwise; yet in that very hour God calls the sufferers “My people.” Zechariah would later say God was “a little angry” while the nations “helped forward the disaster” (Zechariah 1:15). God’s discipline of His own never makes them available for others to exploit. To touch the Lord’s disciplined sheep invites a far greater fury than the trial itself. If He disciplines us, it is as a Father who still calls us His, and “if we are faithless, He remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13).
reflections.q: “Do not enter the gate of My people in the day of their calamity.”

reflections.title: Edom’s Name Is Written on the Day
reflections.html: Three times in one verse: “in the day of their calamity.” The word for calamity, ’ed, with its ending sounds like ’edam, an echo of the name Edom itself. Edom made Judah’s calamity its opportunity, and the prophet lets the nation hear its own name inside the word for the day it exploited. Ten times in verses 11–14 the prophet names Judah’s “day,” preparing for “the day of the LORD” in verse 15. The days we use to profit from another’s pain end up bearing our name. God never lets a calamity be anonymous; He knows who entered the gate.
reflections.q: Three times in one verse: “in the day of their calamity.”

14.brief: The rebuke reaches its lowest point at the crossroads, where Edom waited to cut off those who escaped and delivered up the survivors to the enemy. Those fleeing the attack met further betrayal from their brother nation.
14.explain:
"You should not have stood at the crossroads"

Standing at the crossroads and handing over survivors are the last two of eight things Edom "should not have" done in verses 12–14. Together the eight trace how far Edom went. It began by standing aloof while foreigners attacked Jerusalem (1:11), moved on to gloating and boasting (1:12), and then entered the city and laid hands on its goods (1:13). Here Edom turns against the people who were trying to get away.

The Hebrew word translated "crossroads" describes a place where a road divides, such as a fork in the road or a mountain pass. When a city fell, its people fled any way they could. If the setting is Babylon's conquest, Scripture records that even King Zedekiah and his soldiers slipped out at night and fled by way of the plain, only to be overtaken in the plains of Jericho (2 Kings 25:4–5). Edom knew the roads of the region, and the charge pictures it taking its stand where fleeing people would have to pass.

"To cut off those among them who escaped;"

"Those among them who escaped" are people who had survived the fall of the city and were running for their lives. They had already lost their homes and their capital. Now, at the very moment they thought they might live, they met their own relatives waiting for them.

The verb "cut off" is the same Hebrew word God used for Edom's punishment: "you shall be cut off forever" (1:10), and "everyone from the mountains of Esau may be cut off by slaughter" (1:9). Edom cut off its brother's fugitives, and God declares that Edom itself will be cut off. The punishment matches the crime.

"Nor should you have delivered up those among them who remained"

"Delivered up" means to hand someone over into the power of another, here to the enemy. "Those among them who remained" are the survivors of the attack. Instead of sheltering them, Edom handed them over. Ezekiel describes Edom's guilt in similar terms, saying Edom "shed the blood of the children of Israel by the power of the sword at the time of their calamity" (Ezekiel 35:5).

The same Hebrew verb appears in the Law of Moses: "You shall not give back to his master the slave who has escaped from his master to you" (Deuteronomy 23:15). God commanded His people not to hand over even a runaway slave who came to them for refuge. Edom did the opposite to its own brother nation. It handed over people who had every reason to expect shelter from family. Long before, Amos had condemned Edom because "he pursued his brother with the sword, and cast off all pity" (Amos 1:11). In the day of Jerusalem's calamity, that old hostility showed itself at its worst.

"In the day of distress."

This is the final mention of the "day" that runs through verses 11–14: the day of Judah's calamity, destruction, and distress. "Distress" describes being hemmed in with no way out, which is exactly the situation of the refugees. Edom chose that moment, when its brother was most helpless, to strike.

reflections.title: The Crossroads That Should Have Been a Way Out
reflections.html: “Do not stand at the crossroads to cut off his fugitives.” The word means a parting of the ways, where roads divide, and its only other use is “plunder” (Nahum 3:1). Fugitives fleeing a burning city reached the one place where escape was possible and found their brother waiting with a sword. The crossroads is where help is most possible and most needed. God sets His people at the forks of other people’s roads to open the way, not to close it.
reflections.q: “Do not stand at the crossroads to cut off his fugitives.”

reflections.title: The Cruelty of the Crossroads
reflections.html: Edom set up checkpoints along the escape routes to catch fleeing Judeans and hand them over to Babylon, or sell them into slavery. It positioned itself exactly where Jacob’s survivors were most vulnerable and exploited their lowest moment. Exploiting the vulnerability of an exhausted, fleeing soul is the lowest moral abyss a culture can reach: it blocks the path to mercy for someone running from disaster. We are warned never to use another believer’s season of discipline, failure, or distress to raise ourselves up. When a brother or sister stands at a crossroads of crisis, the carnal response is to capitalize on their weakness or pile on more judgment; the Christlike response is to offer refuge. Do we ever trap people in their past failures, cutting off their avenues of escape and repentance? Who in our lives is standing at a crossroads right now, and are we a barrier or an open road?
reflections.q: Who in our lives is standing at a crossroads right now, and are we a barrier or an open road?

reflections.title: The Receiver Became the Hander-Over
reflections.html: “Do not hand over their survivors in the day of distress.” Amos had already condemned Gaza and Tyre because they “delivered up the whole captivity to Edom” (Amos 1:6, 9); Edom had been the buyer of handed-over captives. Now Edom itself hands survivors over to the enemy, and Psalm 137:7 records its cry that day: “Raze it, raze it, to its very foundation!” A nation that grows used to receiving the fruit of another’s cruelty will in time supply it. What we tolerate as customers we eventually commit as merchants.
reflections.q: “Do not hand over their survivors in the day of distress.”

15.brief: This verse is the hinge of the book: “the day of the LORD upon all the nations is near.” Edom becomes one case within God’s wider judgment, and the governing principle is fitting justice: “As you have done, it shall be done to you,” so that what Edom did will return upon its own head.
15.explain:
"For the day of the LORD upon all the nations is near;"

"The day of the LORD" was a familiar phrase among Israel's prophets. It describes a time when God Himself steps in to judge, bringing down the proud and setting right what has been wrong. Joel cried out, "Alas for the day! For the day of the LORD is at hand; it shall come as destruction from the Almighty" (Joel 1:15). Amos warned Israelites who looked forward to that day, assuming it would only mean trouble for their enemies, that it would be "darkness, and not light" for them as well (Amos 5:18). The prophets spoke of the day of the LORD falling on particular nations at particular times, and they also looked ahead to a final day when God would judge the whole world.

In the verses just before this one, the LORD repeatedly speaks of Judah's "day": the day of their captivity, their destruction, their distress, and three times "the day of their calamity" (verse 13). That was the day Edom took advantage of. It watched, gloated, laid hands on Judah's goods, and cut off those trying to escape, as though Judah's worst day was Edom's opportunity. Now the LORD announces that He has a day of His own. Psalm 137:7 shows how that day of Jerusalem's fall stayed in Israel's memory: "Remember, O LORD, against the sons of Edom the day of Jerusalem, who said, 'Raze it, raze it, to its very foundation!'" Edom thought the day belonged to it, but the final day belongs to the LORD.

This day comes "upon all the nations," not on Edom alone. Edom's judgment is one example of a reckoning that reaches every people who set themselves against God. The word "near" means that this judgment was certain and already approaching. Edom could not count on having more time.

"As you have done, it shall be done to you;"

This is the principle that runs through the whole prophecy. God's judgment on Edom would match what Edom had done. Edom had stood by while strangers carried off Judah's wealth, and its own hidden treasures would be searched out (verse 6). It had turned against its brother, and its own allies would turn against it (verse 7). It had cut off Judah's survivors, and it would be cut off forever (verse 10). Ezekiel gives the same message about Edom: because it rejoiced when Israel's land became desolate, God would make Edom desolate too (Ezekiel 35:15).

Scripture shows this kind of justice elsewhere. When the Canaanite king Adoni-Bezek suffered what he had done to seventy other kings, he admitted, "As I have done, so God has repaid me" (Judges 1:7). Paul states the principle plainly: "Do not be deceived, God is not mocked; for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7). God's judgment is not random or excessive. It fits the wrong done. This does not mean that every hardship a person faces is payback for a specific sin. It means that God sees exactly what the proud and violent have done to others, and He does not let it go unanswered.

"Your reprisal shall return upon your own head."

The Hebrew word translated "reprisal" refers to the way someone has treated others, the harm a person has dealt out. Here that harm comes back on Edom like something thrown that circles back and strikes the one who threw it. The "head" stands for the person himself. David uses the same picture for the wicked man: "His trouble shall return upon his own head, and his violent dealing shall come down on his own crown" (Psalm 7:16).

The one who brings this repayment is God, not Judah. Edom's victims did not have to take revenge, because the LORD had promised to repay. The same truth stands behind Paul's instruction to believers: "Beloved, do not avenge yourselves, but rather give place to wrath; for it is written, 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,' says the Lord" (Romans 12:19).

reflections.title: Their Day, Then His Day
reflections.html: “For the day of the LORD upon all the nations is near.” Ten times in verses 11–14 the prophet spoke of Judah’s “day,” and every one was a day Edom treated as its own. Now comes a different day, with a different owner. “The day of the LORD” names God’s decisive intervention, whether in history or at its end. God has marked an appointment on heaven’s calendar that no nation can move. The injustices against Judah were not overlooked; they were part of a comprehensive reckoning that will reach every proud power. People may have their day over others, and the gloating may last a season, but days do not finally belong to the strongest. The last day belongs to the LORD.
reflections.q: “For the day of the LORD upon all the nations is near.”

reflections.title: The Stone Thrown Upward
reflections.html: “As you have done, it shall be done to you; your reprisal shall return upon your own head.” Edom’s “dealing” is its own deed, coming back like a stone thrown straight up, like the mischief of Psalm 7:16 that “returns upon his own head.” This is the law of the harvest: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7). God’s justice is perfectly symmetrical; the very methods Edom used to torment Israel become the means of its own undoing. Whatever we sow into the lives of others, cruelty, betrayal, theft, or mercy, returns to us, and divine justice makes sinners drink the exact poison they mixed for their brothers. That is a warning, and it is also a comfort: we do not have to settle every score ourselves, because God’s justice is exact (Romans 12:19).
reflections.q: “As you have done, it shall be done to you; your reprisal shall return upon your own head.”

reflections.title: Near and Far in One Picture
reflections.html: Verse 15 widens the view from Edom alone to “all the nations.” If the early date is right, this may be the first mention of the day of the LORD in the Old Testament. Verses 1–14 found a near fulfillment in Edom, while verses 15–21 reach toward the final day. As one scholar put it, Obadiah combines in one picture what history split into different times and events.
reflections.q: Verse 15 widens the view from Edom alone to “all the nations.”

16.brief: The “you” who drank on the LORD’s holy mountain is plural, and readers differ over whether it means Edom and its allies carousing on Mount Zion or Judah drinking the cup of God’s judgment first. Either way, all the nations will go on drinking the cup of the LORD’s judgment until they are “as though they had never been.”
16.explain:
"For as you drank on My holy mountain,"

"For" ties this verse to the warning just given: "the day of the LORD upon all the nations is near," the day when God steps in to judge, and "as you have done, it shall be done to you" (1:15). "My holy mountain" is Mount Zion, Jerusalem's temple hill. God calls it His own. Whatever happened there happened on ground that belonged to Him.

In verse 15 the LORD is still speaking to Edom with a singular "you": "As you have done, it shall be done to you." In verse 16 the "you" changes to plural, so the verse can be read in two ways. It may still be speaking to Edom, now together with those who joined in. If so, the drinking was a victory celebration. After gloating over Judah's ruin and seizing Jerusalem's goods (1:12–13), they drank and celebrated on the very hill where God's temple stood, and their toast would be answered by a very different cup.

The plural may instead turn to God's own people in Judah. Then the drinking is the cup of God's judgment, which Jerusalem drank when the city fell. Isaiah speaks to Jerusalem this way: "You who have drunk at the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury" (Isaiah 51:17). On this reading, the point is that if God did not spare His own people, the nations will not escape. Jeremiah reasons the same way in his prophecy against Edom. If others who did not deserve the cup have had to drink it, Edom will certainly drink it too (Jeremiah 49:12). Either way, the verse moves from what happened on God's mountain to what will happen to every nation.

"So shall all the nations drink continually;"

The "as... so" pattern of verse 15 now reaches beyond Edom to all the nations. Edom's punishment is one part of a judgment that God will bring on the whole world. Throughout the Old Testament, judgment is pictured as a cup of wine that God Himself pours and hands to the guilty. The LORD told Jeremiah, "Take this wine cup of fury from My hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it" (Jeremiah 25:15). The cup is in God's hand, and no nation chooses whether to drink it. "Continually" means the drinking does not stop. No one takes a sip and sets the cup aside.

"Yes, they shall drink, and swallow,"

"Swallow" means to gulp down. The nations will not merely taste God's judgment. They will drain the cup to the bottom, and the repetition stresses that this will surely happen. Jeremiah describes the nations who drink this cup staggering and going mad because of the sword God sends among them (Jeremiah 25:16). If the first drinking was Edom and its allies celebrating on Zion, the reversal is sharp: those who drank in triumph will drink judgment instead. If it was Judah drinking the cup of God's fury, the same cup now passes to all the nations. On either reading, the nations drink judgment to the end.

"And they shall be as though they had never been."

The judgment ends with complete disappearance. Nations that once seemed powerful and permanent will lose their strength and standing so thoroughly that it will be as if they had never existed. This is a sobering word for Edom, which trusted in its mountain strongholds and believed no one could bring it down (1:3). The same holy mountain where the drinking took place will not end in ruin, though. God promises deliverance and holiness there (1:17).

reflections.title: From the Party to the Cup
reflections.html: “For as you drank on My holy mountain, so shall all the nations drink continually.” The first drinking is most likely Edom and its allies carousing in the ruins of Jerusalem, holding drunken feasts on Zion. God turns the image: the second drinking is the cup of His wrath, the prophets’ familiar picture of judgment passed from nation to nation (Jeremiah 25:15–29; 49:12). They will drink the foaming cup until they become as if they had never existed. As one old commentator said, the completion of sin is the commencement of punishment. Those who treat holy things as a party will one day be handed a cup they cannot put down. The LORD is not indifferent to what is poured out on His holy mountain. Have we grown casual in places God calls holy, in worship, at the Lord’s Table, in how we speak of His things?
reflections.q: Have we grown casual in places God calls holy, in worship, at the Lord’s Table, in how we speak of His things?

reflections.title: As If They Had Never Been
reflections.html: “They shall drink, and swallow, and they shall be as though they had never been.” “Swallow” is the gulp of the throat, drinking in full draughts, and the result is not merely defeat but erasure, like the chaff in Daniel’s vision that the wind carried away “so that no trace of them was found” (Daniel 2:35). Nations that seemed permanent can be made to look as if they never were. You simply will not meet an Edomite today. Only one kingdom in this book is promised to last, and no nation builds it.
reflections.q: “They shall drink, and swallow, and they shall be as though they had never been.”

reflections.title: He Drank the Cup So We Could Drink the Other One
reflections.html: “All the nations shall drink continually” the cup of God’s wrath. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed over that very image, “O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will” (Matthew 26:39), and then He drank it to the bottom. Because He swallowed the cup the nations deserved, His people are handed a different cup: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (1 Corinthians 11:25). There are only two cups in Obadiah’s world, and Jesus took the one that was ours. Every communion table is a place where the cup of wrath has already been emptied.
reflections.q: “All the nations shall drink continually” the cup of God’s wrath.

reflections.title: The First Mention of the Holy Mountain
reflections.html: “My holy mountain” is the book’s first mention of Zion, and it sets up the contrast with “the mountain of Esau.” (Some read the first “drinking” as Judah’s cup of discipline, after which the nations drink wrath; either way, the cup comes around.)
reflections.q: “My holy mountain” is the book’s first mention of Zion, and it sets up the contrast with “the mountain of Esau.” (Some read the first “drinking” as Judah’s cup of discipline, after which the nations drink wrath; either way, the cup comes around.)

17.brief: “But on Mount Zion” marks the turn from judgment to hope: the mountain that strangers had overrun will become a place of deliverance and of holiness. The house of Jacob will possess their possessions, recovering the inheritance God gave them.
17.explain:
"But on Mount Zion there shall be deliverance,"

Mount Zion first named the fortified ridge David captured from the Jebusites. Scripture says David "took the stronghold of Zion (that is, the City of David)" and lived there (2 Samuel 5:7, 9). The temple was built later on higher ground just to the north, on Mount Moriah (2 Chronicles 3:1). When Solomon dedicated it, the ark was brought up "from the City of David, which is Zion," and placed in the temple's Most Holy Place (1 Kings 8:1–6). After that, the name Zion came to include the temple hill, where God dwelt among His people, and in time it could stand for Jerusalem as a whole. Obadiah's Mount Zion is the same as God's "holy mountain" in verse 16, the temple hill at the heart of Jerusalem.

"But" sets Zion against what comes just before. All the nations will drink judgment "and they shall be as though they had never been" (1:16), but on this mountain some will be rescued. The same holy mountain that had seen Jerusalem's ruin and humiliation will become the place where God saves.

The Hebrew word for "deliverance" means escape, and it can also refer to the people who escape. It comes from the same root as "those among them who escaped" in verse 14. Edom stood at the crossroads to cut off those fugitives and handed over the survivors to the enemy (1:14). On Mount Zion the LORD Himself will provide escape. Joel gives the same promise: "For in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be deliverance, as the LORD has said, among the remnant whom the LORD calls" (Joel 2:32).

"And there shall be holiness;"

To be holy is to be set apart for God and belong to Him. The phrase can also be translated "it shall be holy," meaning Zion itself. Jerusalem had been defiled. Foreigners had entered its gates and cast lots for it (1:11), and Edom had entered its gate and laid hands on its people's goods (1:13). God promises that His mountain will again be wholly His, no longer trampled by the nations. Joel says the same: "Then Jerusalem shall be holy, and no aliens shall ever pass through her again" (Joel 3:17).

This holiness reaches the people as well as the place. Isaiah speaks of the survivors in Jerusalem: "he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy" (Isaiah 4:3). God does not simply rescue His people and leave them as they were. Those He delivers become a people set apart for Him.

"The house of Jacob shall possess their possessions."

"The house of Jacob" means the people of Israel, the brother nation Edom had wronged (1:10). The Hebrew verb "possess" is the word often used for Israel taking possession of the Promised Land, the inheritance God had promised to Abraham and his descendants (Genesis 17:8). That land had been lost. Invaders had carried off Judah's wealth and its people, and Edom set its eyes on its brother's land. Ezekiel records Edom's boast about Israel and Judah: "These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will possess them" (Ezekiel 35:10).

God reverses that. What others seized will return to its rightful owners, and Jacob's descendants will again hold the inheritance God gave them. The following verses name the regions in every direction that God's people will occupy, including the mountains of Esau (1:19–20). God's purpose is not only to bring Edom down but to bring His own people home to the land He promised them.
17.notes:
The NKJV follows the standard Hebrew text, which reads "shall possess their possessions." In other words, Israel will recover its own inheritance. The written consonants of the Hebrew word translated "their possessions" can also be read with different vowels to mean "those who dispossessed them." The vowel marks printed in the Hebrew text were supplied by later scribes to preserve the traditional reading, which the NKJV follows. On the other reading, Israel takes over the nations that had taken its land. Brenton's English translation of the Septuagint reflects that sense, "the house of Jacob shall take for an inheritance those that took them for an inheritance," and the NRSV follows the same reading.

Verses 19–20 describe God's people taking possession of land that others had seized, including Edom's own mountains, which fits either reading.

reflections.title: The Hinge of the Book
reflections.html: “But on Mount Zion there shall be deliverance.” That “But” turns the whole prophecy, following the denunciations the way Israel’s path through the sea followed Pharaoh’s overthrow. Those who escape share a root with the fugitives Edom cut off at the crossroads (v. 14). Edom shut the road of escape; God makes His own mountain the place of escape. Joel uses the same phrase, “on Mount Zion … there shall be deliverance” (Joel 2:32), the very verse Peter preached at Pentecost: “whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Acts 2:21). The way out that Edom blocked, God opened in Jerusalem.
reflections.q: “But on Mount Zion there shall be deliverance.”

reflections.title: Mount Zion, the Place of Deliverance
reflections.html: Against Edom’s rocky heights stands Zion, God’s chosen mountain. While Mount Esau is wiped clean into desolation, Mount Zion becomes the center of refuge, holiness, and the restoration of covenant inheritance. In the New Covenant, “you have come to Mount Zion … the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). It is our final place of refuge, holiness, and restored inheritance in Christ.
reflections.q: Against Edom’s rocky heights stands Zion, God’s chosen mountain.

reflections.title: Deliverance Means Holiness and Possession
reflections.html: “And it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions.” True deliverance in the kingdom is never mere survival or evacuation from trouble; it is bound up with holiness and restoration. The escape on Mount Zion turns refugees into holy vessels who reclaim their inheritance. Christ does not only rescue us from the consequences of sin; He brings us to His holy hill so we can possess our possessions, stepping fully into the authority, peace, and identity the enemy tried to steal.
reflections.q: “And it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions.”

reflections.title: Possess Your Possessions
reflections.html: “Possess” is the conquest verb of Joshua, used three times in verses 17–20. Picture an Israelite who owns terraces and vineyards and never tastes a grape, or a mill owner who refuses to use the power already supplied to his mill. All things are ours, and yet we live as if nothing were ours. Christ is like a treasure chest that is wholly ours but seldom opened. God has already blessed His people “with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Ephesians 1:3); the inheritance is not in question, only the possessing. Faith is the hand that takes hold of what is already in our name. What has God already given us in Christ that we have not yet taken hold of?
reflections.q: What has God already given us in Christ that we have not yet taken hold of?

reflections.title: Holy Means Inviolable
reflections.html: “It shall be holy”: a sanctuary the nations will no longer dare to trample (compare Joel 3:17). Some translate the last clause, “will dispossess those who dispossessed them,” which fits verses 19–20. The place Edom’s allies partied on becomes a place no one can defile.
reflections.q: “It shall be holy”: a sanctuary the nations will no longer dare to trample (compare Joel 3:17).

18.brief: The LORD pictures the house of Jacob and the house of Joseph, which together appear to describe Judah and the northern tribes, as fire and flame, and the house of Esau as stubble that they burn up. No survivor will remain of the house of Esau as a nation, and the outcome is certain, “For the LORD has spoken.”
18.explain:
"The house of Jacob shall be a fire, And the house of Joseph a flame;"

"The house of Jacob" means the people of Israel, the descendants of Esau's twin brother. "The house of Joseph" points especially to the northern tribes. Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh became the leading tribes of the northern kingdom, which Assyria had carried into exile in 722 BC, long before Judah fell to Babylon. Naming both houses together pictures the whole family of Israel, north and south, restored and standing together again. The prophets looked forward to this reunion, as when Ezekiel joined two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, into one in his hand (Ezekiel 37:15–22).

Israel is pictured as fire, but the power behind that fire belongs to God. Isaiah uses the same kind of picture for God Himself: "So the Light of Israel will be for a fire, And his Holy One for a flame; It will burn and devour His thorns and his briers in one day" (Isaiah 10:17). The people Edom thought it could trample become the means through which God carries out His judgment. The judgment is still God’s own, carried out in His day, as verse 15 has already made clear. The verse gives no one permission to take personal revenge (Romans 12:19).

There is a reversal here. Edom had done violence "against your brother Jacob" (1:10) in the day of Jerusalem's calamity. Now Jacob, the brother Edom wronged, becomes the fire that consumes the house of Esau. Edom is repaid in the same terms as its own conduct.

"But the house of Esau shall be stubble;"

Stubble is the dry stalks left in a field after the harvest. It has no strength and catches fire instantly, so a field of stubble can burn in moments. Edom had trusted in its rugged mountain homeland and its strength, but before God it is nothing more than dry straw. Malachi uses the same image for the day of judgment: "all the proud, yes, all who do wickedly will be stubble. And the day which is coming shall burn them up" (Malachi 4:1).

"They shall kindle them and devour them,"

Fire set to stubble does not stop until everything is gone. Judgment on Edom will not be partial or temporary, and nothing will be left to grow back.

"And no survivor shall remain of the house of Esau,"

The word translated "survivor" is the same word used in verse 14 for those of Judah who "remained" after Jerusalem's fall. Edom had stood at the crossroads to catch those survivors and hand them over to the enemy. Now Edom itself will have no survivors. The contrast with the verse just before is just as sharp: "on Mount Zion there shall be deliverance" (1:17). God's people will have escapees, but Esau's house will have none.

This describes Edom's end as a nation, not the death of every person descended from Esau. Scripture and later history give glimpses of Edom's decline without tying this verse to a single event. By Malachi's day Edom's mountains had been laid waste, though Edom still spoke of rebuilding (Malachi 1:3–4). In later centuries the Nabataeans held its old mountain homeland, and the Edomites who had settled in southern Judah became known as Idumeans. The Jewish historian Josephus reports that in the second century BC the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus conquered the Idumeans and required them to adopt Jewish customs, and that Herod the Great's family came from Idumea. After the first century AD the Idumeans no longer appear as a distinct people, and no nation of Edom exists today. Because Obadiah ties Edom's fall to the day of the LORD upon all the nations (1:15), many interpreters also see a fuller fulfillment still to come.

"For the LORD has spoken."

Obadiah began with "Thus says the Lord GOD concerning Edom" (1:1), and now he closes the judgment the same way. Edom trusted its high cliffs, its wisdom, and its warriors. None of that could stand against what God had said. The outcome was certain because the LORD Himself had declared it.

reflections.title: Fire, Flame, and Stubble
reflections.html: “The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame; but the house of Esau shall be stubble.” The house of Joseph, the northern tribes exiled in 722 B.C., stands beside Judah here: a reunited Israel (Ezekiel 37:16–22) becomes God’s instrument. Stubble does not resist fire; it simply disappears (Malachi 4:1). Isaiah says it is God Himself who “will be for a fire, and His Holy One for a flame” (Isaiah 10:17), so the fire in Israel is God’s own fire carried in His people. The historically oppressed become an unquenchable blaze, while the proud persecutors are exposed as dry, hollow stubble. The old missionary David Brainerd prayed to be a flame of fire in God’s cause. The question is not whether we will be near fire, but whether we will be the flame or the stubble.
reflections.q: “The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame; but the house of Esau shall be stubble.”

reflections.title: The Consuming Unity of the Spirit
reflections.html: Jacob represents the chosen people; Joseph represents the one who suffered and was exalted to save his brothers. Together, as fire and flame, they picture the unified, consuming life of the Spirit. Esau, the flesh, is reduced to stubble. When the Spirit encounters the flesh, the flesh has no substance to withstand it. It has volume, visible presence, and historical weight, but before the pure, blazing reality of Christ’s life it is utterly combustible. It cannot fight the fire; it can only be consumed.
reflections.q: Jacob represents the chosen people; Joseph represents the one who suffered and was exalted to save his brothers.

reflections.title: No Survivor for the House That Handed Over Survivors
reflections.html: “There shall be no survivor of the house of Esau.” “Survivor” is the same word as the “survivors” Edom handed over at the crossroads (v. 14). Edom took away Judah’s survivors; Edom will have no survivor. The vocabulary of the crime has become the vocabulary of the sentence, sealed with “for the LORD has spoken.” History bore it out; after A.D. 70 the Idumeans disappear as a people. (The Greek Old Testament says not even a “fire-bearer” would be left, the torch-bearer who led an army and was customarily spared even in defeat.) God does not need to invent consequences; He lets our own deeds come home.
reflections.q: “There shall be no survivor of the house of Esau.”

reflections.title: A Remnant of Edom at the King’s Feet
reflections.html: Obadiah leaves “no survivor of the house of Esau,” and as a nation Edom did vanish. Yet Amos had promised that David’s restored house would “possess the remnant of Edom, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name” (Amos 9:11–12), and James quoted that passage at the Jerusalem council to show that God was taking from the Gentiles “a people for His name” (Acts 15:14–17). Already in Jesus’ ministry crowds came to Him from Idumea (Mark 3:8). The judgment on Edom’s pride never closed the door of grace to Edom’s people; the King of Zion opened it. No bloodline is too far gone for the Deliverer who comes out of Zion (Romans 11:26).
reflections.q: Obadiah leaves “no survivor of the house of Esau,” and as a nation Edom did vanish.

19.brief: God’s restored people will possess land in every direction: the South will take the mountains of Esau, the Lowland will take Philistia, the fields of Ephraim and Samaria will be possessed, and Benjamin will possess Gilead. The heights from which Edom once looked down will belong to the people it betrayed.
19.explain:
"The South shall possess the mountains of Esau,"

"The South" is the Negev, the dry southern region of Judah that bordered Edom. Its people lived closest to Edom and suffered from its hostility. Now they will take over Edom's rugged mountain homeland, the heights Edom thought no one could reach. The word "possess" is repeated throughout this verse, and it also appears in verse 17: "The house of Jacob shall possess their possessions." It is the word used when Israel entered Canaan under Joshua to take possession of the land God was giving them. The promise describes God giving His people their land once more.

The promise also reverses Edom's ambitions. Ezekiel records that Edom had said of Israel and Judah, "These two nations and these two countries shall be mine, and we will possess them" (Ezekiel 35:10). Edom wanted to take its brother's land. Instead, its brother would hold Edom's mountains. Amos uses related language in his own setting: when God raises up "the tabernacle of David, which has fallen down," His people will "possess the remnant of Edom" (Amos 9:11–12).

"And the Lowland shall possess Philistia."

"The Lowland" is the Shephelah, the low hills between Judah's central highlands and the Mediterranean coast. To the west lay Philistia, the coastal plain of the Philistines. They had been Israel's enemies since the days of the judges, Saul, and David. The people of the foothills would spread down to the coast and claim it.

"They shall possess the fields of Ephraim And the fields of Samaria."

Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom of Israel, and Samaria was its capital. Assyria conquered that kingdom and carried its people into exile, then settled foreigners in their towns (2 Kings 17:6, 24). The verse does not say exactly who "they" are, but it is most naturally the people of Judah. God's restoration would not stop at Judah's own borders. The northern heartland, long lost to foreign rule, would belong to God's people again. The two kingdoms that had divided after Solomon would no longer be separated.

"Benjamin shall possess Gilead."

Gilead was the hill country east of the Jordan River. It was originally given to the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (Joshua 13:8–13), and it was among the first regions lost to Assyria. Benjamin was a small tribe just north of Jerusalem that stayed with Judah when the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:21). Benjamin had a small inheritance, but now it would reach across the Jordan into Gilead.

The verse moves from south to west, then north, then east. The land God first gave to Israel would be recovered on every side, including regions long held by enemies and foreigners. These are real places with real borders, and the promise concerns God restoring His people to them. Obadiah does not say when this will be completely fulfilled. His point is that God's people will not remain scattered and robbed, because He will return to them what He gave them.

reflections.title: The Lowland Takes the Heights
reflections.html: “The South shall possess the mountains of Esau, and the lowland shall possess Philistia.” The people of the Negev, the dry south, the lowest and poorest of Judah’s land, inherit the mountain fortress that boasted no one could climb it; the foothills take the plain of the old enemy. The map then turns north to Ephraim and Samaria and east to Gilead: south, west, north, and east, the four directions promised to Jacob at Bethel, “you shall spread abroad to the west and the east, to the north and the south” (Genesis 28:14). God’s covenant boundaries cannot be cancelled by foreign occupation; the lost inheritance is returned down to the exact boundary stone. The borders here exceed anything the returning exiles held, which is why many look for their fulfillment in Messiah’s kingdom. God’s promises come with place names. The God who keeps His word to Jacob down to the Negev and Gilead will not forget the smallest promise He has made to us.
reflections.q: “The South shall possess the mountains of Esau, and the lowland shall possess Philistia.”

20.brief: Even the exiles are included, for the captives of Israel will possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and the captives of Jerusalem in Sepharad, a place of exile whose location is uncertain, will possess the cities of the South. God’s scattered people will come home to their inheritance.
20.explain:
"And the captives of this host of the children of Israel"

"Host" means a company or band of people. Here it refers to the Israelites who had been carried away from their land. Later in the verse, Obadiah speaks separately of "the captives of Jerusalem," so many interpreters see two groups of exiles here. The first would be the people of the northern kingdom of Israel, whom Assyria deported long before (2 Kings 17:6). The second would be the people of Judah, whose capital was Jerusalem. However long they had been gone, God had not forgotten them. People who had lost everything and lived under foreign rule are the ones He promises to bring back.

"Shall possess the land of the Canaanites As far as Zarephath."

"Possess" is the same word used for Jacob taking possession of what belonged to him (verse 17). It is also the word used when Israel first entered the promised land under Joshua. These returning captives will not live as guests in someone else's territory. They will settle and own the land.

"The land of the Canaanites" here means the coast north of Israel, where the Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon stood. Genesis lists Sidon as the firstborn son of Canaan (Genesis 10:15). Zarephath was a small town on that coast between Tyre and Sidon. It is best known as the place where Elijah stayed with a widow during a famine and raised her son from the dead (1 Kings 17:9–24). By naming Zarephath, God shows that His people's land will reach far to the north, beyond the territories listed in verse 19.

"The captives of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad"

These are people of Judah who had been taken from Jerusalem, most likely after the Babylonian destruction of the city. No one today knows for certain where Sepharad was. What matters is that it was far from home. Even exiles living in a distant land will be brought back. Long before, Moses had promised that if Israel were scattered among the nations and later turned back to the LORD, He would gather them again, even from the farthest places (Deuteronomy 30:1–5). Obadiah shows God keeping that promise. Distance does not put any of His people out of His reach.

"Shall possess the cities of the South."

"The South" is the Negev, the dry region in the southern part of Judah that bordered Edom. Ezekiel records Edom's claim that its brother's land would become its own (Ezekiel 35:10), and Edomites are generally thought to have settled in parts of the Negev after Jerusalem fell. The promise is that Jerusalem's exiles will return and possess the cities of this region. Edom had handed over Judah's survivors (verse 14), but those taken captive will come home and take back what was theirs. A return began after Babylon fell, when exiles went back to Judah under the decree of Cyrus (Ezra 1:1–4). Still, the promise here reaches farther than that early return. It points toward God fully restoring His people in their own land, as verse 21 goes on to describe.
20.notes:
The location of Sepharad is uncertain, and several proposals have been made. One is Sardis, a city in western Asia Minor (modern Turkey). Old Persian inscriptions use a similar name, Sparda, for Sardis and its province.

Others suggest a place in Media, in the east, where northern Israelites had been resettled (2 Kings 17:6).

A long Jewish tradition, going back to an ancient Aramaic translation of the prophets, identified Sepharad with Spain. That is why Jews of Spanish descent are called Sephardic Jews. Whichever place is meant, it was far from Jerusalem.

The first half of the verse is also hard to translate. The Hebrew has no verb there, so the NKJV supplies "shall possess" from the second half.

Another possible reading is "the exiles of Israel who are among the Canaanites as far as Zarephath," meaning captives living in Phoenicia. That reading fits Amos's charge that Gaza and Tyre had delivered up whole populations of captives to Edom (Amos 1:6, 9).

Some scholars have suggested that "this host" was originally the place name Halah, one of the places in Assyria where northern Israelites were deported (2 Kings 17:6). The NRSV adopts that suggestion, reading "The exiles of the Israelites who are in Halah," and its footnote marks this as a correction of the Hebrew, which reads "in this army."

reflections.title: As Far as the Refining Place
reflections.html: “The captives … shall possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath.” Zarephath, on the Phoenician coast between Tyre and Sidon, takes its name from a root meaning “to smelt, to refine.” It is the town where a starving Gentile widow fed Elijah from her last handful of flour (1 Kings 17:9–16), the story Jesus preached at Nazareth (Luke 4:25–26). The restored remnant’s border runs all the way to “the refinery.” The people God brings home are a people who have been through the fire; Zechariah says the remnant will be refined as silver and will call on His name (Zechariah 13:9). God’s map of restoration runs through places of famine and refining, and His grace runs past every border we would draw. (Sepharad, likely Sardis in Asia Minor, later gave the Sephardic Jews their name.) Whatever the places, no exile is too far for God to bring home.
reflections.q: “The captives … shall possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath.”

21.brief: Then deliverers, called “saviors,” will come to Mount Zion to judge the mountains of Esau, much as God once raised up deliverers for Israel in the days of the judges. The book ends with God’s reign rather than Edom’s fall, “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s,” a promise that moves toward God’s universal reign, ultimately fulfilled through Jesus Christ.
21.explain:
"Then saviors shall come to Mount Zion"

The Hebrew word translated "saviors" means deliverers, people God uses to rescue His people from their enemies. It recalls the time of the judges, when Israel cried out under oppression and "the LORD raised up a deliverer for the children of Israel" (Judges 3:9). Men like Othniel, Ehud, and Gideon were not saviors in their own strength. God raised them up, gave them victory, and through them set His people free. Obadiah promises that God will do this again. After the scattering and humiliation described earlier in the prophecy, He will raise up deliverers for His people.

They come to Mount Zion, Jerusalem's temple hill, which God has already promised will be a place of deliverance and holiness (1:17). The Hebrew verb behind "come" literally means to go up. Edom had climbed high in its pride and would be brought down, but these deliverers go up to God's mountain.

"To judge the mountains of Esau,"

The Hebrew word for "judge" means more than issuing a verdict. It also means to govern and to set things right, which is why Israel's deliverers in the book of Judges were called judges. They rescued the people and then led them. Here the deliverers rule over Edom's territory and carry out God's justice there.

The verse sets two mountains side by side. Edom lived in a rugged, lofty homeland and boasted, "Who will bring me down to the ground?" (1:3). Mount Zion, by comparison, was a modest hill. Yet in the end the mountains of Esau are governed from Mount Zion. Edom's heights could not protect it, and the city whose ruin Edom gloated over and whose goods it seized becomes the seat of authority over it. This also echoes what God told Rebekah before her twins were born: "the older shall serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). Esau's descendants had refused to treat Jacob's people as brothers, and now they come under the rule God established on Zion. Obadiah does not say exactly when or how this would be fulfilled, only that it would surely happen.

"And the kingdom shall be the LORD’s."

This is the last line of the book, and it explains everything before it. Edom thought its strength and wisdom made it secure. The nations that overran Jerusalem seemed unstoppable. But neither Edom nor any other nation has the final word. The same God who stirred the nations against Edom (1:1) and whose day of judgment reaches all nations (1:15) is the true King over them all. Even the deliverers on Mount Zion do not rule for themselves. They serve the LORD's kingdom. The psalmist says it the same way: "For the kingdom is the LORD's, and He rules over the nations" (Psalm 22:28).

The deliverers in this verse are human leaders like those God raised up in Israel's past, but the promise reaches beyond them. Each deliverer God gave His people was limited and temporary. Jesus is the Savior and King in whom God's rule over the whole earth reaches its fulfillment. When the seventh trumpet sounds in Revelation, heaven declares, "The kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of His Christ, and He shall reign forever and ever!" (Revelation 11:15). A short prophecy about the judgment of one small nation ends with the truth that the whole world belongs to the LORD.
21.notes:
The NKJV's "saviors" follows the standard Hebrew text, which uses a word meaning "those who deliver." With different vowels, the same consonants can mean "those who have been delivered." The Septuagint reads it that way and also has these rescued people going up from Mount Zion rather than to it, roughly, "those who are rescued shall go up out of Mount Zion." The NET Bible adopts the rescued-people reading but keeps the Hebrew wording about the destination: "Those who have been delivered will go up on Mount Zion." The NRSV is similar: "Those who have been saved shall go up to Mount Zion."

On the rescued-people reading, those who go up would be the survivors promised on Mount Zion in verse 17.

The standard Hebrew reading fits the following phrase, "to judge the mountains of Esau," because judging and governing is what deliverers do.

reflections.title: The Saved Become Saviors
reflections.html: “Then saviors shall come to Mount Zion to judge the mountains of Esau.” “Saviors” comes from the same root as the names Joshua and Jesus; it names the deliverers God raised up to rescue Israel in the days of the Judges (Judges 3:9, 15; Nehemiah 9:27), and the Greek Old Testament translates it “those who have been saved.” “Judge” is the verb of the book of Judges, where deliverers rescued and then governed. Those once hunted at the crossroads now rule from Zion under the King. Those who persevered in brokenness are given authority over the very regions that once enslaved them. The saved are to be saviors. Whoever God delivers, He makes an instrument of deliverance; our rescue is always meant to become someone else’s doorway. How has God’s deliverance made us an instrument of deliverance, and to whom is He sending us now?
reflections.q: How has God’s deliverance made us an instrument of deliverance, and to whom is He sending us now?

reflections.title: The True and Greater Deliverer on Mount Zion
reflections.html: The “saviors” on Mount Zion pointed historically to leaders like Zerubbabel and Nehemiah and the Maccabean deliverers. But the verse finds its true fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the supreme Savior, who went up to Jerusalem, conquered sin and death on Calvary’s hill, and now reigns from the heavenly Jerusalem.
reflections.q: The “saviors” on Mount Zion pointed historically to leaders like Zerubbabel and Nehemiah and the Maccabean deliverers.

reflections.title: Who Are the Deliverers?
reflections.html: Interpreters have heard three answers: the leaders of the return and the Maccabean era; the apostles and ministers of the gospel; and redeemed Israel with the saints reigning with Messiah, which fits the land promises of verses 19–20. And the deliverers “judge” the mountain of Esau in three ways: Edom has no deliverers of its own, the deliverers rule its territory, and they sit in judgment on its sins.
reflections.q: Interpreters have heard three answers: the leaders of the return and the Maccabean era; the apostles and ministers of the gospel; and redeemed Israel with the saints reigning with Messiah, which fits the land promises of verses 19–20.

reflections.title: And the Kingdom Shall Be the LORD’s
reflections.html: The last words of the book are the last word of history: “and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.” In Hebrew it is a short, majestic declaration. Not Edom’s kingdom, and not finally even Israel’s, but His. The line matches Psalm 22:28, “the kingdom is the LORD’s,” and Zechariah 14:9, “the LORD shall be King over all the earth,” and Jewish worship still recites it at the New Year among the texts proclaiming God’s kingship. Human kings fail and fleshly nations fall, but every dynasty, empire, and rogue nation will finally give way to the uncontested, eternal reign of Jesus Christ. People are in His kingdom now, but not all willingly; the day is coming when His reign will be welcomed everywhere. Every “Your kingdom come” ever prayed is traveling toward this sentence. Where are we still building our own small kingdom, and what would it look like to declare over our plans, resources, and future, “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s”?
